_note: Phase F content, written during D because the guide's later beats need something to hang on. Schema from docs/ip-plan-v2.md: { id, kind, title, beats[], needs[] }. kind is main | side | egg | depth. needs[] names line ids that must be complete first, and a gate only exists where the lesson genuinely depends on the earlier one.
_caveat: 240.0.0.0/4 has been reserved since RFC 791, 1981-09, and our own registry confirms it is unallocated - so the line about it is true today. There is a live IETF effort to redesignate it as usable unicast space. If that lands, the line needs rewriting rather than deleting: it becomes a better fact, not a dead one.
_verified: Every fixed address below was checked on 2026-09-18 against apps/ip/data/space.bin - the file this app actually ships - not against an external source. Two claims died in that check and are not in here: 18.0.0.0 is dated 1994 in our registry, not the 1977 the published /8 lists give, so no line claims 1977; and our data carries no holder names at all, so no line names an organisation. Holders arrive from the live lookup and the plate says them. Where a beat needs routing data we do not ship, it is a find[] rule the engine resolves rather than an address I asserted.
_beats: at = a fixed address, verified. find = a rule the sightline engine resolves at runtime, so the chain works without me knowing the answer. say = the guide. teaches = why the beat exists; it is never shown.

lines.title: Where you actually are
lines._note: Reconciles two lists that were never the same list: the seven beats in ip-plan-v2.md say what each step TEACHES, and the eight in ip-emotional-design.md say what each step FEELS. Teaching without a feeling is a curriculum; a feeling without a fact is a caption. Each beat below carries one of each, and the emotional beat is named so a later session cannot quietly drop it.
lines._reframe: Beats 6 and 8 share one sentence VERBATIM - 'Every network decides for itself what to believe' - and it is the only deliberate repetition in the product. At 6 it is the reason nothing is guaranteed. At 8, after the hijack, it is the reason anything works. Nothing new is added; the floor tilts. Edit one and you must edit the other or the ending stops working.
lines._ending: Four words. The emotional design says the bigger the moment the fewer his words, and that the best paragraph at the climax is the failure mode. The flare, the ring and the descent tone stopping carry the rest.

beats.teaches: it is a number, and somebody agreed to it
beats.say: Copied. That number is how the whole internet finds you right now: every reply to everything you do today is addressed to it.
beats.goal: Copy your address

beats.find: the prefix the visitor's address is announced in
beats.teaches: somebody speaks for you
beats.say: This is the block your address belongs to. Your internet provider tells the rest of the internet: send anything for these addresses to me. You are one of them.
beats.goal: Zoom out until you can see the block of addresses yours belongs to

beats.find: another prefix the same network announces
beats.teaches: a network is not one range
beats.say: Same provider, a completely different part of the map. Providers do not own one neat neighbourhood. They collect blocks wherever they can get them, and answer for all of them.
beats.goal: Find another block that belongs to your internet provider

beats.find: the whole of the visitor's address family
beats.teaches: the size, and how little of it is left
beats.say: All of it: every IPv4 address there will ever be, about 4.3 billion. That is fewer than there are people. Nearly all of them are taken, and it still carried everything you did today.
beats.goal: Zoom all the way out, to every IPv4 address there is

beats.find: the whole of the visitor's address family
beats.teaches: the size, and how little of it has been needed
beats.say: All of IPv6: enough for every grain of sand on Earth to have trillions of addresses of its own. Less than a thousandth of the usable part has been handed out so far.
beats.goal: Zoom all the way out, to all of IPv6

beats.teaches: a handful of named things hold the rest up, and people looked after them by hand
beats.say: Every time you type a website’s name, the lookup starts, in principle, at a root server like this one. Thirteen names hold up every name on the internet. And for years the list of who had been given which numbers was kept largely by one man, Jon Postel.
beats.goal: Find the nearest root server, where looking up a website name begins

beats.find: the origin network of any announced prefix
beats.teaches: announcing is a claim, and every listener decides what to do with it
beats.say: Anyone running a network can tell the rest: these addresses are mine. There is no referee. Every network decides for itself what to believe. Some of those claims are checked now. In 2008, none were.
beats.goal: Visit a block run by some other network

beats.teaches: a claim meant for one country escaped
beats.say: In February 2008, Pakistan ordered YouTube blocked. Pakistan Telecom did it by claiming YouTube’s addresses as its own, and the claim leaked out to the world. For about two hours, a lot of the world trying to reach YouTube was sent to Pakistan instead, and got nothing. Nobody meant it to happen.
beats.goal: Go to 208.65.153.0: YouTube, February 2008

beats.find: the whole of the visitor's address family, again
beats.teaches: the same fact, read the other way
beats.say: Every network decides for itself what to believe. And mostly, they agree.
beats.goal: Zoom all the way out one more time

lines.reveal: No one is in charge of the internet’s map. Tens of thousands of networks each decide whose claims to believe, and most of the time they agree well enough to have carried everything you did today.
lines._verified: Rewritten 2026-11-11 for the average person, not a networking person (owner: 'If not interesting to the normal human it is likely noise'). Beats 6 and 8 still share 'Every network decides for itself what to believe' verbatim (see _reframe). 2008: RIPE NCC RIS case study 'YouTube Hijacking' - Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced 208.65.153.0/24 from 18:47 UTC on 24 Feb 2008, propagated by PCCW (AS3491), withdrawn 21:01 UTC: about two hours. RIPE could not measure how much of the internet was affected, so the beat says 'a lot of the world', never 'all'. The Pakistani government's order to block YouTube is widely reported (RIPE, CircleID, APNIC's ISP column 2008-03). 4.3 billion < world population (8+ billion). Under a thousandth of 2000::/3 handed out: 0.0925%, computed from space.bin by scripts/ip-build-door-stats.py. 2^128 / ~7.5e18 grains of sand is ~4.5e19 each, so 'trillions' understates and is true. Jon Postel ran IANA's number assignments until his death in 1998. 'Tens of thousands of networks': RIPE RIS sees over 70,000 originating AS numbers (scripts/ip-build-asn-field.py source). 'In 2008, none were': route origin validation (RPKI) began deployment after 2011.

lines.title: The boundary
lines._note: The plan's beats 6 and 7. The instrument turns around, and the product ends where it should. Fear appeal is the cheapest win available here and taking it would make this a worse product: show how little was kept and let the relief be the payoff. Unblocked 2026-11-11 by a small inward half (js/30-inward.js): what arrived with the visit, what stayed on the device, why it matters, and where sight stops.

beats.find: what actually crossed the wire to get here
beats.teaches: what a visit really reveals
beats.say: Everything I have shown you came from one number and a handful of public registers. Here is all of it.
beats.goal: See what your visit told this site

beats.teaches: your address is not you
beats.say: This is where I stop being able to see. Your address says where to send the answer. It does not say who you are, and I could not tell you.
beats.goal: Read to where this site stops being able to see

lines.reveal: An address is a delivery instruction that a great many strangers have agreed to honour. That is all it is, and it is not nothing.

lines.title: The oldest hands
lines._verified: 1982 is the earliest year present in space.bin. 12.0.0.0/8 is dated 1983 and is a whole /8. 9.0.0.0/8 is dated 1988.

beats.teaches: the record goes back further than people expect
beats.say: Nineteen eighty-two. There is nothing older in the register I carry.
beats.goal: Find the oldest record in the register, at 192.5.21.0

beats.teaches: early allocations were enormous and casual
beats.say: Sixteen million addresses, to one organisation, in one go. The year after the oldest record there is.

beats.teaches: it kept happening for a decade
beats.say: And again. They were not being careless. There was no reason yet to be careful.

lines.reveal: For about ten years the internet was small enough that you could give away sixteen million addresses without anyone needing to think about it.

grants.label: Before 1990
grants.say: You can ask the whole map for old space now. It was always there. You had no way to point at it.

lines.title: Set aside
lines._verified: Rewritten 2026-11-11 for the average person, not a networking person (owner: 'If not interesting to the normal human it is likely noise'). 127.0.0.0/8 loopback: RFC 1122, 16,777,216 addresses; ::1 the single IPv6 loopback, RFC 4291. 192.0.2.0/24 and 2001:db8::/32 are documentation-only (RFC 5737, RFC 3849), the same idea as the 555-01xx numbers US films use. 240.0.0.0/4: 268,435,456 addresses, reserved 'for future use' since the 1980s (RFC 988, 1986, after RFC 791); RFC 3330 records it reserved; still reserved, with an IETF draft (draft-schoen-intarea-unicast-240) unadopted. Equipment that refuses it: RIPE address-policy list and RIPE 88 'Reclaiming 240/4'. 'Billions': 268M x ~$15-20 per address (IPv4Center, CircleID, 2025-26). All four places are landmarks in MARKS.

beats.goal: Go to 127.0.0.1, the address that means “this computer”
beats.teaches: some addresses mean here, not somewhere
beats.say: 127.0.0.1 means “this computer”. Whatever device you are on, this address leads straight back to itself. There is an old joke about it: there’s no place like 127.0.0.1. Sixteen million addresses are set aside to mean nothing but “here”.

beats.goal: Go to ::1, the address that means “this computer”
beats.teaches: some addresses mean here, not somewhere
beats.say: ::1 means “this computer”. Whatever device you are on, this address leads straight back to itself. IPv4 spends sixteen million addresses on meaning “here”. IPv6 spends exactly one.

beats.goal: Go to the internet’s 555 numbers
beats.teaches: space reserved so that examples cannot hit anything real
beats.say: These are the internet’s 555 numbers. Films use fake 555 phone numbers so nobody real gets called by mistake. Manuals and textbooks use addresses from here, so no real computer is ever reached by mistake.

beats.goal: Go to 240.0.0.0, the biggest empty stretch on the map
beats.teaches: space kept back for a future that arrived without it
beats.say: A sixteenth of all IPv4, 268 million addresses, kept back in the 1980s “for future use”. The future came and the world ran out of addresses, and these still sit empty: too much equipment treats them as off-limits. At today’s prices they would be worth billions.

lines.reveal: Not every address is for the internet. Some mean “this computer”, some exist only for examples, and one huge stretch was saved for a future that arrived without it. The world ran short of addresses while these sat set aside.

grants.label: Set-aside space
grants.say: Now you can ask the map to light up every place like these at once.

lines.title: The thirteen
lines._verified: Rewritten 2026-11-11 for the average person, not a networking person (owner: 'If not interesting to the normal human it is likely noise'). Operators from IANA's root server list (iana.org/domains/root/servers), checked 2026-11-11: A and J Verisign; B USC-ISI and D University of Maryland (two universities); E NASA Ames; G US DoD; H US Army Research Lab; I Netnod (Sweden); K RIPE NCC (Amsterdam); M WIDE Project (Japan); C Cogent; F ISC; L ICANN - twelve organisations. Verisign runs .com. 'About two thousand machines': root-servers.org showed 2,048 operational instances on 2026-11-11; ICANN's RSSAC FAQ says more than 1,500. The old third beat (the same letter in the other family) needed the doors and is replaced by K.

beats.goal: Find root server A
beats.teaches: what a root server is for
beats.say: Root server A. When you type a website’s name, finding it starts, in principle, with a server like this, which points the way to .com, .org and every other ending. A is run by Verisign, the company that also runs .com.

beats.goal: Find root server E
beats.teaches: the thirteen are deliberately run by different hands
beats.say: Root server E is run by NASA. Others are run by the US Army, two universities, a Swedish organisation and a Japanese research project: twelve organisations, deliberately different, so that no single failure can take the internet’s names down.

beats.goal: Find root server K
beats.teaches: thirteen is a number of names, not machines
beats.say: K is run from Amsterdam. And “thirteen servers” is only thirteen names: each one is really many copies spread around the world, about two thousand machines in all, and your lookups go to whichever copy is nearest.

lines.reveal: Thirteen names, twelve organisations and about two thousand machines hold up every website name you have ever typed. It works because nobody owns all of it.

grants.label: The thirteen
grants.say: Now you can ask the map to light up all thirteen at once, wherever you are standing.

lines.title: Sold, and given back
lines._verified: Checked 2026-11-11. LIVE (RIPEstat network-info): 18.0.0.0/16 announced by AS3, MIT; 18.200.0.0/16 and 18.130.0.0/16 by AS16509, Amazon; 36.0.0.0 not announced. space.bin: 36.0.0.0/8 is APNIC, all of it handed out in 2011, about 70% registered to China (CN), the rest ID, JP, TW, NP. MIT's sale: Network World, 'MIT selling 8 million coveted IPv4 addresses; Amazon a buyer' (2017); Internet Society blog, 'MIT goes on IPv4 selling spree' (May 2017) - sale proceeds to fund MIT's network upgrade. Stanford: IANA IPv4 address-space registry history, 36/8 Stanford, returned to IANA as reserved 2000-07, allocated to APNIC 2010-10 (NANOG and APNIC announcements, October 2010; Geoff Huston's 36/8 study). Stanford's stated reason was not found, so no line gives one. Price: IPv4Center 2025 report, average $27.75 per address over 2025; CircleID and IPv4Center put early-2026 averages near $20; /16-sized blocks traded below $15. 'Hundreds of millions of dollars' for 16.8 million addresses holds at any of these ($250M at $15). No line names an exact figure, because the price moves.

beats.goal: Go to 18.0.0.0, one of the first blocks ever handed out
beats.teaches: a founding-era block, held by one university
beats.say: MIT's. Sixteen million addresses, given to one university back when the internet was a research project. MIT still answers for this end of it.

beats.goal: Now go to the other half: 18.200.0.0
beats.teaches: addresses became property, and were sold
beats.say: Same block, and Amazon answers here. In 2017 MIT sold millions of addresses it was not using, and spent the money on its own network. Addresses had run out, so they had become worth buying.

beats.goal: Go to 36.0.0.0, the block that was given back
beats.teaches: the opposite decision, and where the space went
beats.say: This was Stanford's, all sixteen million. In 2000 Stanford handed the whole block back, for nothing. Ten years later it was given out again, across Asia, most of it to networks in China.

lines.reveal: Once there were no more addresses, the old ones became property. One university sold millions of its spare ones; another gave its whole block away, which at today's prices of around twenty dollars an address would be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Where a block is registered today says very little about where it started.
lines._note: Rewritten 2026-11-11 for an ordinary reader (owner: 'If not interesting to the normal human it is likely noise. Not your average networking person, but the average person'). The hook is money and generosity, which everyone understands: one university sold its spare addresses, another gave them away. The old draft's claim that 36/8 went to 'a registry that did not exist when it was first handed out' was dropped: the register dates Stanford's block 1993, the year APNIC began, and nothing found says otherwise.

lines.title: Small countries, old space
lines._verified: Computed from space.bin 2026-09-18: Singapore holds 27,894,080 v4 addresses of which 66.0% were allocated before 1993, the highest share of any country holding over a million. North Korea holds one range of 1,024 addresses.

beats.teaches: share of old space has nothing to do with size
beats.say: Two thirds of this was handed out before 1993. Of every country holding more than a million addresses, none has a larger share that old.
beats.goal: Ask the map for everything registered to Singapore

beats.teaches: the other end of the same scale
beats.say: One range. A thousand addresses, for a country.
beats.goal: Now ask it for North Korea

lines.reveal: How much of this is registered to a country says almost nothing about how large the country is, and a great deal about how early the people asking for it got there.

lines.title: The quiet ones
lines._note: Half authored, half computed - the template from docs/ip-story-research.md. The engine supplies the addresses because we cannot know them in advance; only the meaning is written.

beats.find: allocated before 2000, and nothing announces it
beats.teaches: old and silent is a real and common state
beats.say: Somebody was given these addresses before 2000, and today nothing on the internet leads here. They are not empty. They belong to someone. They have gone quiet.
beats.goal: Find addresses given out before 2000 that the internet cannot reach today

beats.teaches: it is not a one-off
beats.say: Another, from a different handout. Not a fluke, then.
beats.goal: Find another, from a different handout
Go to 11.0.0.0, which was quiet for decades
beats.teaches: quiet is not forgotten
beats.say: This is the Pentagon’s, and much of its space sat dormant for decades. On 20 January 2021, minutes after a new US president was sworn in, a company nobody had heard of began announcing it to the world: 175 million addresses by April. The Pentagon later said it had arranged it, to see who was using its addresses. Today it announces them itself.

lines.reveal: Some of the dark on this map is not empty. It was handed out decades ago and went quiet: still taken, but not answering. And quiet does not mean forgotten. In 2021, 175 million of the Pentagon’s quiet addresses woke up overnight.
lines._verified: Rewritten 2026-11-11 for the average person, not a networking person (owner: 'If not interesting to the normal human it is likely noise'). The 2021 story: Doug Madory (Kentik) traced the first announcement by AS8003 (Global Resource Systems LLC, Plantation, Florida) to 16:57 UTC on 20 Jan 2021, minutes after the inauguration; 56 million addresses by late January, 175 million by mid-April; the Pentagon's Defense Digital Service called it a pilot to assess and prevent unauthorised use (AP / Washington Post, April 2021; SecurityWeek, SiliconANGLE); in September 2021 the announcements moved to DoD's own operations. LIVE 2026-11-11 (RIPEstat): 11.0.0.0/24, 21.0.0.0/8, 22.0.0.0/16, 26/8, 28/8, 30/8 announced by AS749 (DoD Network Information Center). IPv4 only: IPv6 allocations before 2000 are too rare to find.

lines.title: Where the map is wrong
lines._note: Gated for a real reason, not an arbitrary one: a block announced from the wrong continent is not STRANGE until you have watched an ordinary network's footprint stay where it was put. Entirely computed - it needs live routing data we do not ship.

beats.find: a prefix whose registered country differs from the country its origin network is registered under
beats.teaches: the register records paperwork, not geography
beats.say: Registered under one country. Announced by a network registered under another. Neither of them is lying.
beats.goal: Find a block registered in one country but run by a network registered in another

beats.find: a second one, in a different registry
beats.teaches: it is structural, not an error
beats.say: Again, and nothing is wrong. This is what the two records are for.
beats.goal: Find another, under a different registry

lines.reveal: One record says which country the paperwork was filed under. The other says which network is announcing it. People read the first as a map of where the machines are, and it was never that - and this is two records disagreeing, not a measurement of anywhere.
lines._gate: Was gated on the-quiet-ones, which is now IPv4 only and would have locked IPv6 visitors out forever. The plan's own reason for the gate is 'a network is not one range', which is beat 3 of the main line, so the main line is the gate.

_grants: Finishing a chain can teach the map a new way of being looked at. The owner's report after days of wandering: 'I go, and then nothing happens.' A line of text is not a consequence. A lens is - it changes what the whole field shows from then on, it compounds, and hour five is richer than hour one. Nothing is invented: the data is already on the device and the lens is permission to ask for it. Only chains whose lens is computable offline grant one.
_rules: What the engine (js/29-chains.js) checks for each beat. `find` stays the human description; `rule` is the machine test, so a new chain made of existing rules is rows only. at: the place answered contains the beat's address (at6 for an IPv6 visitor; a beat in the other family is skipped). copied: the visitor copied their address. own-block: the view pulled back to the block they are announced in. same-network: arrived at another block their own network announces. whole-family: the view pulled all the way out. root: arrived at any root server. other-origin: arrived at a block announced by a network other than theirs. query-cc: asked the map for that country. quiet: arrived somewhere allocated before 2000 that nothing announces, in an allocation not already used for this line. cc-mismatch: arrived at a block whose registered country differs from its origin network's (one RIPEstat lookup by AS number), under a registry not already used for this line. inward-open: opened 'What your visit told this site'. inward-edge: read down to where this site's sight stops. other-family: not reachable yet (the doors) and skipped. soft: may be passed silently when the next beat is met. goal: the tracker's one line.
